plan.topic_summary: Supervised fine-tuning (SFT) is a core post-training technique for adapting large language models to specific tasks and domains. For a 1–5 year view, the key question is whether SFT remains a durable, high-value step in the model pipeline or is being displaced by alternative alignment methods, in-context learning, and parameter-efficient approaches that shift cost and moat dynamics.
key_questions: How are companies currently deploying SFT in production, and what use cases are driving the most revenue or strategic value?
What is the current cost structure of SFT relative to pre-training and inference, and how is it trending as model sizes grow?
To what extent are alternative post-training methods (RLHF, DPO, constitutional AI) displacing SFT as the primary alignment step, and what does that mean for SFT-specific tooling and data businesses?
How is the quality and availability of high-quality SFT data evolving, and what are the main bottlenecks (labeling cost, domain expertise, privacy)?
Will parameter-efficient fine-tuning (LoRA, adapters) commoditize SFT into a low-margin utility, or will data curation and evaluation remain a defensible moat?
How do data privacy regulations and model extraction risks affect the viability of SFT as a commercial offering, particularly for regulated industries?

sources.title: #InsTag: Instruction Tagging for Analyzing Supervised Fine-tuning of Large Language Models
sources.abstract: Foundation language models obtain the instruction-following ability through supervised fine-tuning (SFT). Diversity and complexity are considered critical factors of a successful SFT dataset, while their definitions remain obscure and lack quantitative analyses. In this work, we propose InsTag, an open-set fine-grained tagger, to tag samples within SFT datasets based on semantics and intentions and define instruction diversity and complexity regarding tags. We obtain 6.6K tags to describe comprehensive user queries. Then we analyze popular open-sourced SFT datasets and find that the model ability grows with more diverse and complex data. Based on this observation, we propose a data selector based on InsTag to select 6K diverse and complex samples from open-source datasets and fine-tune models on InsTag-selected data. The resulting models, TagLM, outperform open-source models based on considerably larger SFT data evaluated by MT-Bench, echoing the importance of query diversity and complexity. We open-source InsTag in https://github.com/OFA-Sys/InsTag.

sources.title: Rotation-Preserving Supervised Fine-Tuning
sources.abstract: Supervised fine-tuning (SFT) improves in-domain performance but can degrade out-of-domain (OOD) generalization. Prior work suggests that this degradation is related to changes in dominant singular subspaces of pretrained weight matrices. However, directly identifying loss-sensitive directions with Hessian or Fisher information is computationally expensive at LLM scale. In this work, we propose preserving projected rotations in pretrained singular subspaces as an efficient proxy for Fisher-sensitive directions, which we call Rotation-Preserving Supervised Fine-Tuning (RPSFT). RPSFT penalizes changes in the projected top-$k$ singular-vector block of each pretrained weight matrix, limiting unnecessary rotation while preserving task adaptation. Across model families and sizes trained on math reasoning data, RPSFT improves the in-domain/OOD trade-off over standard SFT and strong SFT baselines, better preserves pretrained representations, and provides stronger initializations for downstream RL fine-tuning. Code is available at \href{https://github.com/jinhangzhan/RPSFT.git}{https://github.com/jinhangzhan/RPSFT}.

sources.title: Anchored Supervised Fine-Tuning
sources.abstract: Post-training of large language models involves a fundamental trade-off between supervised fine-tuning (SFT), which efficiently mimics demonstrations but tends to memorize, and reinforcement learning (RL), which achieves better generalization at higher computational cost. Dynamic Fine-Tuning (DFT) recently emerged as a promising middle ground, reweighting SFT objectives with token probabilities and achieving improvements in certain reasoning domains, though it exhibits instability in other tasks. We provide a analysis of DFT through the reward-weighted regression (RWR) framework, revealing that it corresponds to a specific auxiliary distribution choice that yields provably tighter RL bounds than standard SFT. However, our analysis also uncovers a critical limitation: this construction lacks distributional anchoring, leading to progressive drift that undermines training stability. To address this, we propose Anchored Supervised Fine-Tuning (ASFT), which augments DFT's reweighting with lightweight KL regularization to preserve tightness while ensuring stability. Empirically, ASFT consistently outperforms both SFT and DFT across mathematical reasoning, medical knowledge grounding, and code generation, achieving substantial improvements with minimal computational overhead. Our RWR framework provides a systematic lens for understanding post-training methods and demonstrates that principled theoretical analysis leads to both stronger guarantees and practical gains. The code is available at https://github.com/zhuchichi56/ASFT.

sources.title: Supervised Fine-Tuning as Inverse Reinforcement Learning
sources.abstract: The prevailing approach to aligning Large Language Models (LLMs) typically relies on human or AI feedback and assumes access to specific types of preference datasets. In our work, we question the efficacy of such datasets and explore various scenarios where alignment with expert demonstrations proves more realistic. We build a sequential decision-making framework to formulate the problem of aligning LLMs using demonstration datasets. Drawing insights from inverse reinforcement learning and imitation learning, we introduce various approaches for divergence minimization in the LLM alignment tasks. Our analysis highlights the mass-covering and mode-seeking behaviors of these different approaches. Inclusively, we examine the pros and cons of the classical supervised fine-tuning method, elaborating on scenarios where different methods shine.

sources.title: A Mechanistic Investigation of Supervised Fine Tuning
sources.abstract: The cosine similarity between a large language model's hidden activations before and after Supervised Fine-Tuning (SFT) remains very high. This, at first glance, suggests that SFT leaves the model's activation geometry largely undisturbed. However, projecting both sets of activations through a Sparse Autoencoder (SAE) pretrained on the base model reveals that the underlying sparse latents diverge significantly. We introduce a novel investigative pipeline which utilizes these pretrained SAEs as a high-resolution diagnostic tool to mechanistically investigate the drivers of this representational divergence. Through our analytical pipeline, we discover task-specific and layer-specific distributions of the precise semantic features that are systematically altered during supervised fine-tuning. We additionally identify a layer-wise update profile specific to safety alignment. All code, experimental scripts, and analysis files associated with this work are publicly available at: https://github.com/ruhzi/sae-investigation.

sources.title: Rethinking Data Selection for Supervised Fine-Tuning
sources.abstract: Although supervised finetuning (SFT) has emerged as an essential technique to align large language models with humans, it is considered superficial, with style learning being its nature. At the same time, recent works indicate the importance of data selection for SFT, showing that finetuning with high-quality and diverse subsets of the original dataset leads to superior downstream performance. In this work, we rethink the intuition behind data selection for SFT. Considering SFT is superficial, we propose that essential demonstrations for SFT should focus on reflecting human-like interactions instead of data quality or diversity. However, it is not straightforward to directly assess to what extent a demonstration reflects human styles. Towards an initial attempt in this direction, we find selecting instances with long responses is surprisingly more effective for SFT than utilizing full datasets or instances selected based on quality and diversity. We hypothesize that such a simple heuristic implicitly mimics a crucial aspect of human-style conversation: detailed responses are usually more helpful.

sources.title: Towards Pedagogical LLMs with Supervised Fine Tuning for Computing Education
sources.abstract: This paper investigates supervised fine-tuning of large language models (LLMs) to improve their pedagogical alignment in computing education, addressing concerns that LLMs may hinder learning outcomes. The project utilised a proprietary dataset of 2,500 high quality question/answer pairs from programming course forums, and explores two research questions: the suitability of university course forums in contributing to fine-tuning datasets, and how supervised fine-tuning can improve LLMs' alignment with educational principles such as constructivism. Initial findings suggest benefits in pedagogical alignment of LLMs, with deeper evaluations required.

sources.title: Supervised Fine‐tuning
Labeling supervised fine-tuning data with the scaling law
sources.abstract: This paper introduces a multi-stage manual annotation calibrated by the scaling law, offering a high-quality Supervised Fine-Tuning data acquisition method for environments with constrained resources like GPU poor, limited GPT access, and funding restrictions. We have preprocessed 58k authentic chat data and manually annotated 2.3k questions. After this, we conducted fine-tuning on Qwen models, ranging from 0.5B to 32B parameters. The optimal version improved 29.07 in F1 score. This confirms the viability of fine-tuning Large Language Model (LLM) for downstream Natural Language Processing (NLP) tasks. Our contributions are: 1) Created Supervised Fine-Tuning (SFT) training data in alpaca format, along with a set of Low-Rank Adaptation (LoRA) weights, and 2) Developed a method for acquiring high-quality data leveraging scaling law principle. The script, raw data with alpaca format and experiments track are open-sourced on Github (https://github.com/InternLM/HuixiangDou/tree/main/web/tools), HuggingFace (https://huggingface.co/tpoisonooo) and WandB (https://wandb.ai/tpoisonooo/huixiangdou-cr/table?nw=nwusertpoisonooo). The privacy of the data involved has been authorized by users. SFT data and license comes from ncnn contributors group.

sources.title: RASFT: Rollout-Adaptive Supervised Fine-Tuning for Reasoning
sources.abstract: Supervised fine-tuning (SFT) is a prevailing method for adapting large language models to reasoning tasks by imitating offline expert demonstrations, often treating a single expert trajectory as the target behavior. However, reasoning is not simple path imitation: rigidly following one demonstrated solution may overfit to surface forms and suppress the model's own reasoning distribution. We propose Rollout-Adaptive Supervised Fine-Tuning (RASFT), a policy-aware SFT framework that calibrates expert supervision according to problem-level solvability estimated from verified on-policy rollouts. For each problem, RASFT strengthens expert guidance when the current policy struggles, while relaxing rigid imitation and incorporating correct self-generated trajectories when the model already exhibits reliable reasoning behavior. To preserve useful reasoning priors, RASFT further introduces a clipped inverse ratio between the frozen reference model and the current policy to constrain excessive policy drift. Experiments across multiple models on six mathematical reasoning benchmarks and two code reasoning benchmarks show that RASFT achieves better overall performance than SFT, SFT variants, and representative RL methods. The code is available at https://github.com/zjd1sq/RASFT.

sources.title: ASFT: Aligned Supervised Fine-Tuning through Absolute Likelihood
sources.abstract: Direct Preference Optimization (DPO) is a method for enhancing model performance by directly optimizing for the preferences or rankings of outcomes, instead of traditional loss functions. This approach has proven effective in aligning Large Language Models (LLMs) with human preferences. Despite its widespread use across various tasks, DPO has been criticized for its sensitivity to the effectiveness of Supervised Fine-Tuning (SFT) and its limitations in enabling models to learn human-preferred responses, leading to less satisfactory performance. To address these limitations, we propose Aligned Supervised Fine-Tuning (ASFT), an effective approach that better aligns LLMs with pair-wise datasets by optimizing absolute likelihood for each response, rather than using the Bradley-Terry model, and eliminates the need for a reference model. Through theoretical gradient analysis, we demonstrate that ASFT mitigates the issue where the DPO loss function decreases the probability of generating human-dispreferred data at a faster rate than it increases the probability of producing preferred data. Additionally, we compare ASFT to DPO and its latest variants, such as the single-step approach ORPO, using the latest instruction-tuned model Llama3, which has been fine-tuned on UltraFeedback and HH-RLHF. We evaluated performance on instruction-following benchmarks like MT-Bench and traditional text generation metrics such as BLEU-4 and ROUGE-L. Extensive experiments demonstrate that ASFT is an effective alignment approach, consistently outperforming existing methods.

sources.title: Token Cleaning: Fine-Grained Data Selection for LLM Supervised Fine-Tuning
sources.abstract: Recent studies show that in supervised fine-tuning (SFT) of large language models (LLMs), data quality matters more than quantity. While most data cleaning methods concentrate on filtering entire samples, the quality of individual tokens within a sample can vary significantly. After pre-training, even in high-quality samples, patterns or phrases that are not task-related can be redundant, uninformative, or even harmful. Continuing to fine-tune on these patterns may offer limited benefit and even degrade downstream task performance. In this paper, we investigate token quality from a noisy-label perspective and propose a generic token cleaning pipeline for SFT tasks. Our method filters out uninformative tokens while preserving those carrying key task-specific information. Specifically, we first evaluate token quality by examining the influence of model updates on each token, then apply a threshold-based separation. The token influence can be measured in a single pass with a fixed reference model or iteratively with self-evolving reference models. The benefits and limitations of both methods are analyzed theoretically by error upper bounds. Extensive experiments show that our framework consistently improves downstream performance. Code is available at https://github.com/UCSC-REAL/TokenCleaning.

sources.title: Teaching AI to Handle Exceptions: Supervised Fine-Tuning with Human-Aligned Judgment
sources.abstract: Large language models (LLMs), initially developed for generative AI, are now evolving into agentic AI systems, which make decisions in complex, real-world contexts. Unfortunately, while their generative capabilities are well-documented, their decision-making processes remain poorly understood. This is particularly evident when testing targeted decision-making: for instance, how models handle exceptions, a critical and challenging aspect of decision-making made relevant by the inherent incompleteness of contracts. Here we demonstrate that LLMs, even ones that excel at reasoning, deviate significantly from human judgments because they adhere strictly to policies, even when such adherence is impractical, suboptimal, or even counterproductive. We then evaluate three approaches to tuning AI agents to handle exceptions: ethical framework prompting, chain-of-thought reasoning, and supervised fine-tuning. We find that while ethical framework prompting fails and chain-of-thought prompting provides only slight improvements, supervised fine-tuning - specifically with human explanations - yields markedly better results. Surprisingly, in our experiments, supervised fine-tuning even enabled models to generalize human-like decision-making to novel scenarios, demonstrating transfer learning of human-aligned decision-making across contexts. Furthermore, fine-tuning with explanations, not just labels, was critical for alignment, suggesting that aligning LLMs with human judgment requires explicit training on how decisions are made, not just which decisions are made. These findings highlight the need to address LLMs' shortcomings in handling exceptions in order to guide the development of agentic AI toward models that can effectively align with human judgment and simultaneously adapt to novel contexts.

sources.title: Unveiling the Secret Recipe: A Guide For Supervised Fine-Tuning Small LLMs
sources.abstract: The rise of large language models (LLMs) has created a significant disparity: industrial research labs with their computational resources, expert teams, and advanced infrastructures, can effectively fine-tune LLMs, while individual developers and small organizations face barriers due to limited resources. In this paper, we aim to bridge this gap by presenting a comprehensive study on supervised fine-tuning of LLMs using instruction-tuning datasets spanning diverse knowledge domains and skills. We focus on small-sized LLMs (3B to 7B parameters) for their cost-efficiency and accessibility. We explore various training configurations and strategies across four open-source pre-trained models. We provide detailed documentation of these configurations, revealing findings that challenge several common training practices, including hyperparameter recommendations from TULU and phased training recommended by Orca. Key insights from our work include: (i) larger batch sizes paired with lower learning rates lead to improved model performance on benchmarks such as MMLU, MTBench, and Open LLM Leaderboard; (ii) early-stage training dynamics, such as lower gradient norms and higher loss values, are strong indicators of better final model performance, enabling early termination of sub-optimal runs and significant computational savings; (iii) through a thorough exploration of hyperparameters like warmup steps and learning rate schedules, we provide guidance for practitioners and find that certain simplifications do not compromise performance; and (iv) we observed no significant difference in performance between phased and stacked training strategies, but stacked training is simpler and more sample efficient. With these findings holding robustly across datasets and models, we hope this study serves as a guide for practitioners fine-tuning small LLMs and promotes a more inclusive environment for LLM research.

sources.title: Proximal Supervised Fine-Tuning
sources.abstract: Supervised fine-tuning (SFT) of foundation models often leads to poor generalization, where prior capabilities deteriorate after tuning on new tasks or domains. Inspired by trust-region policy optimization (TRPO) and proximal policy optimization (PPO) in reinforcement learning (RL), we propose Proximal SFT (PSFT). This fine-tuning objective incorporates the benefits of trust-region, effectively constraining policy drift during SFT while maintaining competitive tuning. By viewing SFT as a special case of policy gradient methods with constant positive advantages, we derive PSFT that stabilizes optimization and leads to generalization, while leaving room for further optimization in subsequent post-training stages. Experiments across mathematical and human-value domains show that PSFT matches SFT in-domain, outperforms it in out-of-domain generalization, remains stable under prolonged training without causing entropy collapse, and provides a stronger foundation for the subsequent optimization.

sources.title: Preserving Diversity in Supervised Fine-Tuning of Large Language Models
sources.abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) typically rely on Supervised Fine-Tuning (SFT) to specialize in downstream tasks, with the Cross Entropy (CE) loss being the de facto choice. However, CE maximizes the likelihood of observed data without accounting for alternative possibilities. As such, CE usually leads to reduced diversity in the model's outputs, which hinders further development that requires sampling to explore better responses. To address this limitation, this paper introduces a new game-theoretic formulation for SFT. In this framework, an auxiliary variable is introduced to regulate the learning process. We prove that the proposed game-theoretic approach connects to the problem of reverse KL minimization with entropy regularization. This regularization prevents over-memorization of training data and promotes output diversity. To implement this framework, we develop GEM, a new training algorithm that is computationally efficient as CE by leveraging some unique properties of LLMs. Empirical studies of pre-trained models from 3B to 70B parameters show that GEM achieves comparable downstream performance to CE while significantly enhancing output diversity. This increased diversity translates to performance gains in test-time compute scaling for chat and code generation tasks. Moreover, we observe that preserving output diversity has the added benefit of mitigating forgetting, as maintaining diverse outputs encourages models to retain pre-trained knowledge throughout the training process.

sources.title: An Empirical Study of Catastrophic Forgetting in Large Language Models During Continual Fine-Tuning
sources.venue: IEEE Transactions on Audio Speech and Language Processing
sources.abstract: Catastrophic forgetting (CF) is a phenomenon that occurs in machine learning when a model forgets previously learned information while acquiring new knowledge for achieving satisfactory performance in downstream tasks. As large language models (LLMs) have demonstrated remarkable performance, it is intriguing to investigate whether CF exists during the continual instruction tuning of LLMs. This study empirically evaluates the forgetting phenomenon in LLMs' knowledge during continual instruction tuning from the perspectives of domain knowledge, reasoning, and reading comprehension. The experiments reveal that catastrophic forgetting is generally observed in LLMs ranging from 1b to 7b parameters. Surprisingly, as the model scale increases, the severity of forgetting intensifies in such a model scale range, which may result from the much more significant initial performance in the larger LLM. The finding is also observed by the experiment of Qwen-2.5-Inst from 3B to 14B. Comparing the decoder-only model BLOOMZ with the encoder-decoder model mT0, BLOOMZ exhibits less forgetting and retains more knowledge. Interestingly, we also observe that LLMs can mitigate language biases, such as gender bias, during continual fine-tuning. Furthermore, our findings indicate that general instruction tuning can help alleviate the forgetting phenomenon in LLMs during subsequent fine-tuning.

sources.title: Bayesian Parameter-Efficient Fine-Tuning for Overcoming Catastrophic Forgetting
sources.venue: IEEE/ACM Transactions on Audio Speech and Language Processing
sources.abstract: We are motivated primarily by the adaptation of text-to-speech synthesis models; however we argue that more generic parameter-efficient fine-tuning (PEFT) is an appropriate framework to do such adaptation. Nevertheless, catastrophic forgetting remains an issue with PEFT, damaging the pre-trained model's inherent capabilities. We demonstrate that existing Bayesian learning techniques can be applied to PEFT to prevent catastrophic forgetting as long as the parameter shift of the fine-tuned layers can be calculated differentiably. In a principled series of experiments on language modeling and speech synthesis tasks, we utilize established Laplace approximations, including diagonal and Kronecker-factored approaches, to regularize PEFT with the low-rank adaptation (LoRA) and compare their performance in pre-training knowledge preservation. Our results demonstrate that catastrophic forgetting can be overcome by our methods without degrading the fine-tuning performance, and using the Kronecker-factored approximation produces a better preservation of the pre-training knowledge than the diagonal ones.

sources.title: Dynamic Orthogonal Continual Fine-tuning for Mitigating Catastrophic Forgettings
sources.abstract: Catastrophic forgetting remains a critical challenge in continual learning for large language models (LLMs), where models struggle to retain performance on historical tasks when fine-tuning on new sequential data without access to past datasets. In this paper, we first reveal that the drift of functional directions during the fine-tuning process is a key reason why existing regularization-based methods fail in long-term LLM continual learning. To address this, we propose Dynamic Orthogonal Continual (DOC) fine-tuning, a novel approach that tracks the drift of these functional directions and dynamically updates them during the fine-tuning process. Furthermore, by adjusting the gradients of new task parameters to be orthogonal to the tracked historical function directions, our method mitigates interference between new and old tasks. Extensive experiments on various LLM continual learning benchmarks demonstrate that this approach outperforms prior methods, effectively reducing catastrophic forgetting and providing a robust tool for continuous LLM fine-tuning. Our code is available at https://github.com/meloxxxxxx/DOC.

sources.title: CURLoRA: Stable LLM Continual Fine-Tuning and Catastrophic Forgetting Mitigation
sources.abstract: This paper introduces CURLoRA, a novel approach to fine-tuning large language models (LLMs) that leverages CUR matrix decomposition in the context of Low-Rank Adaptation (LoRA). Our method addresses two critical challenges in LLM fine-tuning: mitigating catastrophic forgetting during continual learning and reducing the number of trainable parameters. We propose a unique modification to the CUR decomposition process, utilizing inverted probabilities for column and row selection which acts as an implicit regularization, and initializing the U matrix as a zero matrix, and only fine-tuning it. We demonstrate through experiments on multiple datasets that CURLoRA outperforms standard LoRA in mitigating catastrophic forgetting. It maintains model stability and performance across tasks while significantly reducing the number of trainable parameters. Our results show that CURLoRA achieves very good and stable task accuracy while maintaining base model's perplexity scores fixed compared to LoRA upon continual fine-tuning, particularly in scenarios with limited data.

sources.title: Parameter Efficient Fine-tuning of Self-supervised ViTs without Catastrophic Forgetting
sources.venue: IEEE/CVF Conference on Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition Workshops (CVPRW)
sources.abstract: Artificial neural networks often suffer from catastrophic forgetting, where learning new concepts leads to a complete loss of previously acquired knowledge. We observe that this issue is particularly magnified in vision transformers (ViTs), where post-pre-training and fine-tuning on new tasks can significantly degrade the model’s original general abilities. For instance, a DINO ViT-Base/16 pre-trained on ImageNet-1k loses over 70% accuracy on ImageNet-1k after just 10 iterations of fine-tuning on CIFAR-100. Overcoming this stability-plasticity dilemma is crucial for enabling ViTs to continuously learn and adapt to new domains while preserving their initial knowledge. In this work, we study two new parameter-efficient fine-tuning strategies: (1) Block Expansion, and (2) Low-rank adaptation (LoRA). Our experiments reveal that using either Block Expansion or LoRA on self-supervised pre-trained ViTs surpass fully fine-tuned ViTs in new domains while offering significantly greater parameter efficiency. Notably, we find that Block Expansion experiences only a minimal performance drop in the pre-training domain, thereby effectively mitigating catastrophic forgetting in pre-trained ViTs1.

sources.title: Dynamic Orthogonal Continual Fine-tuning for Mitigating Catastrophic Forgetting of LLMs
sources.abstract: Catastrophic forgetting remains a critical challenge in continual learning for large language models (LLMs), where models struggle to retain performance on historical tasks when fine-tuning on new sequential data without access to past datasets. In this paper, we first reveal that the drift of functional directions during the fine-tuning process is a key reason why existing regularization-based methods fail in long-term LLM continual learning. To address this, we propose Dynamic Orthogonal Continual (DOC) fine-tuning, a novel approach that tracks the drift of these functional directions and dynamically updates them during the fine-tuning process. Furthermore, by adjusting the gradients of new task parameters to be orthogonal to the tracked historical function directions, our method mitigates interference between new and old tasks. Extensive experiments on various LLM continual learning benchmarks demonstrate that this approach outperforms prior methods, effectively reducing catastrophic forgetting and providing a robust tool for continuous LLM fine-tuning.

sources.title: Improved Supervised Fine-Tuning for Large Language Models to Mitigate Catastrophic Forgetting
sources.abstract: Supervised Fine-Tuning (SFT) is a critical step for enhancing the instruction-following capabilities of Large Language Models (LLMs) and adapting them to specialized domains. However, SFT often leads to a degradation of the model's general abilities, a phenomenon known as catastrophic forgetting. This problem is exacerbated when third-party practitioners fine-tune open-source models, as the original SFT data is typically not available. To address this challenge, we propose a novel and cost-effective SFT method that effectively mitigates catastrophic forgetting without requiring access to the original SFT data. Our approach first reconstructs the likely instruction distribution of the base model. It then employs a multi-model generation and filtering pipeline to synthesize a high-quality general-purpose dataset. This synthetic dataset is mixed with new, domain-specific data for fine-tuning. Experimental results show that our method not only preserves the model's capabilities in general domains but also improves task-specific performance, outperforming baselines that use publicly available SFT datasets.

sources.title: Overcoming Catastrophic Forgetting for Fine-Tuning Pre-trained GANs
Fine Tuning without Catastrophic Forgetting via Selective Low Rank Adaptation
sources.abstract: Adapting deep learning models to new domains often requires computationally intensive retraining and risks catastrophic forgetting. While fine-tuning enables domain-specific adaptation, it can reduce robustness to distribution shifts, impacting out-of-distribution (OOD) performance. Pre-trained zero-shot models like CLIP offer strong generalization but may suffer degraded robustness after fine-tuning. Building on Task Adaptive Parameter Sharing (TAPS), we propose a simple yet effective extension as a parameter-efficient fine-tuning (PEFT) method, using an indicator function to selectively activate Low-Rank Adaptation (LoRA) blocks. Our approach minimizes knowledge loss, retains its generalization strengths under domain shifts, and significantly reduces computational costs compared to traditional fine-tuning. We demonstrate that effective fine-tuning can be achieved with as few as 5\% of active blocks, substantially improving efficiency. Evaluations on pre-trained models such as CLIP and DINO-ViT demonstrate our method's broad applicability and effectiveness in maintaining performance and knowledge retention.

sources.title: NADS: Navigator-Guided Data Selection for Mitigating Catastrophic Forgetting in Fine-Tuning
sources.abstract: Catastrophic forgetting is a central obstacle in single-stage fine-tuning of large language models (LLMs) on a new task, especially when the original pretraining data are unavailable. Synthetic data offers a practical mitigation path, but candidate pools are often noisy and redundant, making effective selection essential. Existing methods often rely on indirect proxy signals whose alignment with actual training benefit can be limited, while utility--diversity selection over large candidate pools remains computationally demanding. To address these challenges, we propose NAvigator-guided Data Selection (NADS), a fine-tuning framework for LLMs. NADS first follows the target fine-tuning recipe without preservation regularization to obtain a navigator model, whose deviation from the pretrained model exposes recipe-induced capability drift. It then uses the predictive divergence between the navigator and the pretrained model to score forgetting-aware utility for each synthetic candidate, and constructs a constraint set through an efficient utility--diversity selection strategy. Finally, NADS fine-tunes on the new-task data while distilling pretrained behavior on the selected constraints to preserve general capabilities. Experiments show that NADS delivers a stronger balance between new-task performance and general capability preservation, while reducing utility--diversity selection overhead. Code at: https://github.com/zjh-vinky/NADS.

sources.title: Overcoming Catastrophic Forgetting in Visual Continual Learning with Reinforcement Fine-Tuning
sources.abstract: Recent studies suggest that Reinforcement Fine-Tuning (RFT) is inherently more resilient to catastrophic forgetting than Supervised Fine-Tuning (SFT). However, whether RFT (e.g., GRPO) can overcome forgetting in challenging visual continual learning settings, such as class-incremental learning (CIL) and domain-incremental learning (DIL), remains an open problem. Through a pilot study, we confirm that while RFT consistently outperforms SFT, it still suffers from non-negligible forgetting. We empirically trace this bottleneck to Trajectory-level Drift Agnosticism: among candidate rollouts achieving identical task rewards, the KL divergence from the preceding-task policy varies substantially, which strongly correlates with catastrophic forgetting across sequential tasks. Motivated by this insight, we propose Retention-aware Policy Optimization (RaPO), a simple yet effective RFT method that mitigates forgetting through trajectory-level reward shaping. Specifically, RaPO comprises two core components: (1) Retention Reward that converts trajectory-level distribution drift into a continuous reward signal, preferentially reinforcing knowledge-preserving rollouts; (2) Cross-Task Advantage Normalization (CTAN), which maintains a persistent exponential moving average of reward statistics across task boundaries to stabilize the optimization progress during continual learning. Leveraging the free-form textual generalization of MLLMs, we comprehensively evaluate RaPO across five visual continual learning settings. Extensive experiments demonstrate that RaPO achieves leading performance, substantially reducing catastrophic forgetting while preserving strong plasticity. To the best of our knowledge, this work represents the first systematic exploration of RFT in visual continual learning, offering insights that we hope will inspire future research. Code is available at https://github.com/LMMMEng/RaPO.

sources.title: Mitigating Catastrophic Forgetting With Adaptive Transformer Block Expansion in Federated Fine-Tuning
sources.abstract: Federated fine-tuning (FedFT) of large language models (LLMs) has emerged as a promising solution for adapting models to distributed data environments while ensuring data privacy. Existing FedFT methods predominantly utilize parameter-efficient fine-tuning (PEFT) techniques to reduce communication and computation overhead. However, they often fail to adequately address the catastrophic forgetting, a critical challenge arising from continual adaptation in distributed environments. The traditional centralized fine-tuning methods, which are not designed for the heterogeneous and privacy-constrained nature of federated environments, struggle to mitigate this issue effectively. Moreover, the challenge is further exacerbated by significant variation in data distributions and device capabilities across clients, which leads to intensified forgetting and degraded model generalization. To tackle these issues, we propose FedBE, a novel FedFT framework that integrates an adaptive transformer block expansion mechanism with dynamic trainable-block allocation. Specifically, FedBE expands trainable blocks within the model architecture, structurally separating newly learned task-specific knowledge from the original pre-trained representations. Additionally, FedBE dynamically assigns these trainable blocks to clients based on their data distributions and computational capabilities. This enables FedBE to better accommodate heterogeneous federated environments and enhances the generalization ability of the model. Extensive experiments show that compared with existing federated fine-tuning methods, FedBE achieves 12-74% higher accuracy retention on general tasks after fine-tuning and a model convergence acceleration ratio of 1.9-3.1× without degrading the accuracy of downstream tasks.

findings.claim: Catastrophic forgetting is a general, empirically observed side effect of continual instruction tuning of LLMs, not an edge case. The evidence covers small-to-mid-size models.
findings.label: verified_fact
findings.rationale: One empirical study (abstract only), peer-reviewed in an IEEE journal. Coverage is limited to roughly 1B-14B models, so it says nothing direct about frontier-scale models.
findings.supporting_excerpt: The experiments reveal that catastrophic forgetting is generally observed in LLMs ranging from 1b to 7b parameters.

findings.claim: Forgetting severity increased with model size in the tested range, so scaling up the base model may not reduce this risk. The authors suggest the effect may partly reflect the larger models' higher starting performance, which would make it partly a measurement artifact.
findings.label: verified_fact
findings.rationale: Single study. The abstract reports the scale trend only up to 14B (Qwen-2.5-Inst 3B-14B) and offers a tentative explanation. Whether the trend holds at larger scale is a gap, not a finding.
findings.supporting_excerpt: Surprisingly, as the model scale increases, the severity of forgetting intensifies in such a model scale range, which may result from the much more significant initial performance in the larger LLM.

findings.claim: SFT can degrade a model's general abilities. The problem is worse for third-party practitioners who fine-tune open-source models without the original SFT data, which limits their ability to replay or regularize against the base model's distribution.
findings.label: verified_fact
findings.rationale: Both are arXiv preprints (not peer reviewed). They state the problem as motivation and propose their own fixes, which rely on synthetic data reconstruction. The risk statement comes from the authors' framing, not an independent measurement.
findings.supporting_excerpt: SFT often leads to a degradation of the model's general abilities, a phenomenon known as catastrophic forgetting.

findings.claim: Parameter-efficient methods such as LoRA are not a complete fix for forgetting. Several papers propose new variants because standard LoRA and prior regularization methods still forget. Each paper claims it outperforms its chosen baselines, and no common benchmark links them.
findings.label: ai_interpretation
findings.rationale: Synthesis across abstracts. src_473b51b4b5 says forgetting persists with PEFT, src_5ec28dd2b6 reports beating standard LoRA, and src_c351319fe2 says regularization-based methods fail in long-term continual learning. Three of the four are arXiv preprints. The mix of baselines and benchmarks cannot be compared from abstracts alone, so the fixes' relative merit is unverified.

findings.claim: Mitigation methods may trade extra complexity or compute for retention. NADS must first run an unregularized fine-tune to obtain a 'navigator' model. Other approaches add synthetic data pipelines, gradient tracking, or architecture expansion.
findings.label: ai_interpretation
findings.rationale: Inferred from method descriptions in abstracts. NADS describes a multi-step procedure, and its abstract admits that utility-diversity selection over large candidate pools 'remains computationally demanding'. Total cost versus plain SFT is not quantified in these abstracts, so this is a possible overhead, not a measured one. Most sources are preprints.

findings.claim: Forgetting appears in vision models as well as LLMs, and can be severe. One example is a DINO ViT-Base/16 losing over 70% ImageNet-1k accuracy after only 10 fine-tuning iterations on CIFAR-100.
findings.label: verified_fact
findings.rationale: A single illustrative example from a workshop paper, in a deliberately stressful setup (small new dataset, full fine-tuning). It should not be generalized to typical fine-tuning practice. The same paper says LoRA and Block Expansion reduce the problem.
findings.supporting_excerpt: For instance, a DINO ViT-Base/16 pre-trained on ImageNet-1k loses over 70% accuracy on ImageNet-1k after just 10 iterations of fine-tuning on CIFAR-100.

findings.claim: Reinforcement fine-tuning (RFT) is discussed as a more forgetting-resistant alternative to SFT, but the evidence shows it does not eliminate forgetting. This is a displacement risk for SFT that is only partial and so far unproven.
findings.label: verified_fact
findings.rationale: One arXiv preprint (not peer reviewed), limited to visual continual learning. The abstract is truncated, so the full evaluation scope is unknown. It cites 'recent studies' on RFT's resilience without detail.
findings.supporting_excerpt: Through a pilot study, we confirm that while RFT consistently outperforms SFT, it still suffers from non-negligible forgetting.

findings.claim: Federated fine-tuning of LLMs may intensify forgetting because client data distributions and device capabilities vary. PEFT-based federated methods are described as inadequate on this point.
findings.label: unverified_claim
findings.rationale: This is the authors' motivating statement in a paper proposing FedBE. The abstract gives no quantitative evidence for it, so it is treated as an unverified premise.
findings.supporting_excerpt: Moreover, the challenge is further exacerbated by significant variation in data distributions and device capabilities across clients, which leads to intensified forgetting and degraded model generalization.

hype_flags: 'Overcoming' or 'without' catastrophic forgetting: titles and abstracts claim full resolution, but these are usually relative improvements over chosen baselines on specific benchmarks.
'Without degrading the fine-tuning performance' (Bayesian PEFT): a strong claim from one abstract, tested on language modeling and speech synthesis only.
'Extensive experiments' and 'robust tool' (DOC): no numbers or benchmark names in the abstract, and the claims come from authors' own method papers.
'RFT is inherently more resilient than SFT': the pilot study in src_905142aa6b still finds non-negligible forgetting.
Parameter-efficiency framing (e.g., 'as few as 5% of active blocks'): efficiency gains do not show equal retention across tasks, models or distribution shifts.

finding.claim: S1 and S2 are presented as parallel findings, but they point in opposite directions on what makes SFT data effective. S1 says diversity and complexity matter. S2 says quality and diversity selection is beaten by a simple long-response heuristic. The findings do not reconcile this. Both rest on single preprints that were evaluated on different benchmarks. S1's headline result is measured with MT-Bench, a benchmark that may reward long, detailed answers, which could confound the two readings.
finding.label: ai_interpretation
finding.rationale: InsTag reports success on MT-Bench with 6K selected samples. The Rethinking paper argues that quality and diversity selection is no better than a response-length heuristic. A style- or length-sensitive evaluation could explain part of S1's gain, but the abstracts do not test this. The conflict is therefore unresolved, and the two findings should not be read as cumulative support for data selection.

finding.claim: S1 is labelled verified_fact and generalised as 'diversity and complexity correlate with model ability'. The abstract supports only an observational correlation across open-source datasets, plus a single selector result. The comparison is against 'open-source models based on considerably larger SFT data', and the abstract does not control for base model, training recipe or evaluator. Evaluation is by MT-Bench alone, which is an LLM-judged benchmark. The result is a 2023 preprint and is not evidence of a causal mechanism.
finding.label: ai_interpretation
finding.rationale: The excerpt shows a single benchmark and a comparison to models trained on other data. It does not establish that data selection is the only difference, and it supports only the correlation. The finding needs a caveat on causality and on reliance on a single LLM-judged benchmark.
finding.supporting_excerpt: outperform open-source models based on considerably larger SFT data evaluated by MT-Bench, echoing the importance of query diversity and complexity.
finding.guard_note: relabelled ai_interpretation: a challenge is a judgement; its quoted excerpt was checked against the source

finding.claim: S3 repeats the paper's own unqualified claim of 'consistent downstream improvement' from token cleaning. The abstract gives no model sizes, benchmarks or effect sizes. It also notes that the two token-influence variants have 'limitations'. The iterative variant uses self-evolving reference models, so compute cost and the risk of error accumulation are not stated. S3 also frames this as a field-wide push toward token-level selection, but it cites a single preprint.
finding.label: ai_interpretation
finding.rationale: The excerpt is the authors' own claim, with no quantified results in the abstract. A 'trend' based on one paper is an overreach. The abstract also does not compare the method with sample-level selection baselines, and S2 suggests that a trivial heuristic could be competitive.
finding.supporting_excerpt: Extensive experiments show that our framework consistently improves downstream performance.
finding.guard_note: relabelled ai_interpretation: a challenge is a judgement; its quoted excerpt was checked against the source

finding.claim: S4 and S5 describe a 'converging' cluster of drift-control methods as if they were corroborating each other. Each is a separate preprint, with no cited_by counts, that reports gains over its own chosen baselines. The domains are mostly math reasoning, with some code and medical tasks. The methods have not been compared head-to-head. The abstracts do not show whether the gains hold at scale, in general chat, or outside the math and code evaluations. The risk side (R4) shows that many similar forgetting-mitigation papers make the same kind of self-selected-baseline claim.
finding.label: ai_interpretation
finding.rationale: The excerpt is a self-reported comparison against baselines the authors chose. Several of these papers are 2025–2026 preprints that have not been cited or replicated. Conceptual similarity between the methods is not independent confirmation of the effect. GEM is reported as 'comparable' to CE in-domain, so for that method the benefit is diversity rather than accuracy.
finding.supporting_excerpt: RPSFT improves the in-domain/OOD trade-off over standard SFT and strong SFT baselines

finding.claim: S8 reports that RASFT beats 'representative RL methods', and S5 reports gains over SFT and DFT. Both come from single-author-group preprints with abstract-only evidence. The abstracts do not say whether the RL baselines were tuned equivalently, and RASFT needs verified on-policy rollouts, which add much of the compute cost that SFT normally avoids. The finding labelled 'SFT variant' is therefore closer to an RL-hybrid approach, and its advantage over SFT may reflect the extra rollout compute.
finding.label: ai_interpretation
finding.rationale: The excerpt is the authors' summary, with no compute-matched comparison. The method needs rollouts and a verifier, so it applies only to tasks with verifiable answers (math and code). This limits how far the result generalises to ordinary SFT.
finding.supporting_excerpt: RASFT achieves better overall performance than SFT, SFT variants, and representative RL methods.

finding.claim: S9 and S12 generalise from narrow settings. S9's 'generalize to novel scenarios' comes from a single preprint on a specific exception-handling task, and the abstract says 'in our experiments', so the claim should not be extended to agentic systems in general. For S12, the pedagogical study uses a proprietary dataset of 2,500 Q&A pairs, so it cannot be replicated, and its authors say 'deeper evaluations required'. Grouping these as evidence of a trend toward domain alignment overstates them.
finding.label: ai_interpretation
finding.rationale: The excerpt shows the education result is preliminary. S9 also compares SFT with human explanations against prompting only, and not against other tuning methods, so the claim that SFT is better does not carry over to alternatives.
finding.supporting_excerpt: Initial findings suggest benefits in pedagogical alignment of LLMs, with deeper evaluations required.
finding.guard_note: relabelled ai_interpretation: a challenge is a judgement; its quoted excerpt was checked against the source

finding.claim: S10's hyperparameter guidance is stated as general but comes from small models (3B to 7B) across four open-source bases. The abstract says it challenges TULU and Orca recipes, but it does not show the findings hold for larger models, other data mixes or LoRA. 'Early training signals predict better performance' is a correlation that may depend on the specific setup. The benchmarks cited (MMLU, MTBench, Open LLM Leaderboard) are public and may be contaminated.
finding.label: ai_interpretation
finding.rationale: The excerpt shows the scope is limited to 3B–7B models, so S10 needs a scope caveat. Whether the recipe transfers to larger models is not addressed in the abstract.
finding.supporting_excerpt: We focus on small-sized LLMs (3B to 7B parameters) for their cost-efficiency and accessibility.
finding.guard_note: relabelled ai_interpretation: a challenge is a judgement; its quoted excerpt was checked against the source

finding.claim: The Science findings mostly report gains in SFT from data selection, regularisation, and policy-style objectives without a core caveat: SFT itself degrades general ability, and the findings S4, S5 and S8 address this only partially. Catastrophic forgetting is documented as a general effect in LLMs from 1B to 7B, and severity increased with model size in the tested range. The findings on data selection (S1–S3), on hyperparameters (S10) and on low-resource SFT (S11) say nothing about forgetting and general-capability loss. This makes them look more favourable to SFT than the evidence supports.
finding.label: ai_interpretation
finding.rationale: The excerpt shows that SFT can reduce general abilities, which the data-selection and hyperparameter findings do not discuss. Benchmarks such as MT-Bench or an F1 score on one downstream task would not detect such loss.
finding.supporting_excerpt: SFT often leads to a degradation of the model's general abilities, a phenomenon known as catastrophic forgetting.
finding.guard_note: relabelled ai_interpretation: a challenge is a judgement; its quoted excerpt was checked against the source

finding.claim: S11 reports a '29.07 F1 improvement' with no baseline, task definition, or error bars, and the abstract gives it as a bare number ('improved 29.07 in F1 score'). The paper does not say whether this is absolute points or relative, or which model size gave the best result. The data set is 2.3k manually labelled questions from a single community (ncnn contributors). Treating this as evidence for a scaling-law-calibrated method is unsupported. The scaling-law claim is not shown to be better than ordinary annotation.
finding.label: ai_interpretation
finding.rationale: The excerpt gives a single number with no baseline and an 'optimal version' selected from models of 0.5B to 32B, so selection effects are likely. The result shows that SFT works for a niche task, not that the annotation method does.
finding.supporting_excerpt: The optimal version improved 29.07 in F1 score. This confirms the viability of fine-tuning Large Language Model (LLM) for downstream Natural Language Processing (NLP) tasks.
finding.guard_note: relabelled ai_interpretation: a challenge is a judgement; its quoted excerpt was checked against the source

finding.claim: S6 and S7 give mechanistic and theoretical framings more weight than the abstracts support. S6 is a diagnostic study whose abstract reports divergence in SAE latents, but it does not show that this divergence causes degradation, and SAEs trained on the base model may not represent the fine-tuned model faithfully. S7 calls SFT 'reframed' as policy optimisation, but this is a conceptual lens in three separate papers with different formalisms, and not an established consensus. One of them (the IRL paper) explicitly examines 'pros and cons of the classical supervised fine-tuning method' and does not claim SFT is replaced.
finding.label: ai_interpretation
finding.rationale: The excerpt shows an observation of latent divergence, not a link to capability loss. SAE fidelity after fine-tuning is not discussed in the abstract. The 'reframing' is a modelling choice and not a result.
finding.supporting_excerpt: projecting both sets of activations through a Sparse Autoencoder (SAE) pretrained on the base model reveals that the underlying sparse latents diverge significantly.

limitations: Analysis is based on abstracts only, and one paper (src_aa99ae42eb) has no abstract, so no claim about it can be made beyond its title.
Most mitigation papers are arXiv preprints and not peer reviewed. Several are by their authors' own method proposals and are not independent replications.

All 12 papers concern catastrophic forgetting, so risks of SFT outside it (data quality, alignment or safety erosion, overfitting, annotation cost, hallucination from new knowledge) are not covered by this set.
Evidence covers models up to about 14B parameters and some vision models. Frontier-scale and proprietary fine-tuning services are not covered.
No paper provides compute cost, reproducibility details or cross-method benchmarks in its abstract, so relative merit of mitigations cannot be judged.
The set contains duplicate versions (DOC appears twice), so the effective number of independent studies is smaller than 12.
No company, supplier or commercial deployment data appear in the papers, so no company-level risk was assessed.
Only titles, metadata and abstracts were available, so details such as effect sizes, baselines and ablations could not be checked.
Most cited papers are 2024–2026 preprints with few or no citations, so I could not judge replication or peer-review status.
I did not search for papers that directly test the contradictions I flag, for example whether MT-Bench length bias explains the InsTag result.
Challenges to S4, S5 and S8 are partly interpretation of how comparable the reported baselines are, and not shown contradictions.

sources.title: SYSTEMS AND METHODS FOR ENHANCING LARGE LANGUAGE MODEL RELIABILITY WITH HALLUCINATION AVERSE FINE-TUNING AND DETECTION [US20260359628A1]
sources.abstract: A method may include: receiving, by a computer program, pairs of conversation text and summaries; generating, by the computer program, training data by injecting hallucinations into the conversation text or the summaries; fine-tuning, by the computer program, a large language model (LLM) with the generated training data using a loss function; providing, by the computer program, validation conversation text to the fine-tuned LLM; generating, by the computer program, a lookback ratio vector comprising attention paid by the fine-tuned LLM to content at each token generation step; extracting, by the computer program, token probabilities at each layer of the fine-tuned LLM into a logit-based vector; concatenating, by the computer program, the lookback ratio vector and the logit-based vector; classifying, by the computer program, the concatenated lookback ratio vector and the logit-based vector using a logistic regression classifier; and deploying, by the computer program, the LLM to a production environment.

sources.title: ENHANCED DECISION MAKING THROUGH FEW-SHOT ADAPTATION OF ARTIFICIAL INTELLIGENCE MODELS FOR ACTION DETECTION [US20260360102A1]
sources.abstract: Systems and methods for enhanced decision making through few-shot adaptation of artificial intelligence models for action detection. Augmented feature maps can be obtained by injecting feature augmentations of detected features from video frames into a feature space of a vision encoder of a machine learning model. The vision encoder can be trained to learn low rank adaptation parameters based on the augmented feature maps. Entity level features can be extracted from the video frames by performing region of interest alignment on the augmented feature maps obtained by the vision encoder injected with low rank adaptation (LoRA) parameters. Similarity between the entity level features and action text embeddings obtained from the video frames can be maximized by minimizing an alignment loss to train the machine learning model and obtain an optimized machine learning model for performing downstream tasks.

sources.title: INTEGRATED MULTI-DOMAIN SYSTEM FOR AUTONOMOUS CORROSION AND DEGRADATION MANAGEMENT USING PREDICTIVE ANALYTICS AND MULTI-LAYER RADIO COMMUNICATION [WO2026234434A1]
sources.abstract: An Integrated Corrosion Monitoring and Treatment System (ICMTS) is introduced for multi-domain application. The system features a versatile sensor network for physical, chemical, and biomedical parameters, and self-healing microcapsules for autonomous repair. An AI-driven processing unit uses hybrid CNN-LSTM architectures for predictive analytics. A multi-layer radio communication subsystem supports LF, HF, UHF, VHF, Sub-GHz, Wi-Fi, ZigBee, UWB, 5G, Bluetooth, LoRa, and SatCom protocols. It utilizes UAVs, helipads, micro-drones, and smartphones as mobile edge gateways for resilient data relay, remote tracking, and secure two-way control in inaccessible areas. A hybrid energy management system ensures continuous operation. The ICMTS integrates real-time monitoring, predictive analytics, and autonomous repair into a single platform for industrial, aerospace, medical, veterinary, civil engineering structures (including those made of concrete, steel, and wood), and smart infrastructure domains. The scope of the system is not limited to aforementioned applications and encompasses structures and materials susceptible to corrosion and degradation.

sources.title: SYSTEMS AND METHODS FOR PERSONALIZING A VIRTUAL AGENT TRAINED USING AN ARTIFICIAL INTELLIGENCE (AI) MODEL [US20260359564A1]
sources.abstract: A computer implemented method is provided for automatically generating a textual response to a message using a trained artificial intelligence (AI) model. The method includes receiving a request to customize the trained AI model and initiating a training phase comprising parsing the request to generate a set of fine-tuning parameters. The fine-tuning parameters include one or more of (i) a contextual prompt configured to capture a guardrail for specifying a desired subject matter within which the response falls, and (ii) a vector-based representation of a desired tone for the response. The method further includes generating the textual response to the message by inputting the message and the set of fine-tuning parameters into the trained AI model.

sources.title: RETRACTABLE TRAILER HITCH SYSTEMS AND METHODS [US20260356142A1]
sources.abstract: A hitch system can include a ball hitch and an actuator. The actuator can be operated to cause the ball hitch to extend and retract. The ball hitch can include a ball mount and a shank. The hitch system can further include a sleeve configured to telescopingly receive at least a portion of the shank. In this manner, a position of the ball hitch can be adjusted with respect to a towing vehicle for “fine tuning” a position of the ball hitch when coupling, decoupling, and/or moving a towed vehicle (e.g., a trailer).

sources.title: SYSTEMS AND METHODS FOR JOINT FINE-TUNING AND COMPRESSION OF NEURAL NETWORKS [WO2026235215A1]
sources.abstract: A method and system are provided for constructing neural network models optimized for reduced computational resource usage. A weight matrix of a neural network layer is represented as a parameterized, compressible data structure comprising learnable parameters. A composite objective function is determined, including a task loss component measuring predictive performance and a compression loss component penalizing resource usage characteristics such as parameter dimensionality, sparsity, or numerical precision, for the neural network model. The neural network model is iteratively optimized with respect to the composite objective function using gradient-based updates to the compressible structure. The resulting model achieves both accuracy and efficiency objectives during a shared optimization process. The optimized compressible data structure may be adapted for different target tasks, enabling task-specific architectures with reduced inference cost. The trained neural network model is deployable in various environments without reliance on fixed, pretrained components used during optimization.

sources.title: GENERATIVE MODEL-AUGMENTED DATA CURATION WITH MULTI-STAGE EVALUATION AND PREFERENCE-BASED FINE-TUNING [US20260359613A1]
sources.abstract: A system and method are disclosed for a data curation process that integrates generative models, automated evaluators, and iterative refinement workflows. Input seeds, comprising structured metadata and domain-specific attributes, are evaluated against predefined criteria to generate augmented input-output pairs. These pairs undergo multi-stage evaluation and annotation processes involving corrections, metadata additions, and structured feedback to ensure quality, relevance, and compliance with user-defined standards. Annotated pairs are validated using additional evaluators before being used to train generative models, optimizing their outputs for subsequent tasks. Preference data is dynamically generated across stages to fine-tune models and evaluators, while failed examples are used to generate unit test cases for improving evaluation frameworks. The system incorporates iterative feedback loops to refine input seeds, augmentation prompts, and evaluation criteria, enabling scalable, efficient, and high-quality data curation workflows adaptable to diverse tasks and requirements.

sources.abstract: [0000]    A contactless service confirmation system for portable sanitation assets utilizing RF technologies such as RFID, BLE, WiFi, LoRa or others. Each portable unit is embedded with a tamper-proof RF tag. Technicians' service tools are equipped with RF readers that detect proximity to the tag, automatically logging timestamps and service durations. A control module with sensors and wireless communication facilitates real-time monitoring and cloud-based analytics. The system ensures tamper-proof, automated service verification, improves recordkeeping, and enhances accountability with minimal technician interaction.

sources.title: Method of collecting contextual behavioral data within digital narrative intelligence environments [US12792581B1]
sources.abstract: A computer-implemented narrative intelligence system and method for managing digital artifacts and harvesting contextualized collaborator behaviors to support AI-assisted information management and model training. Content and collaborator interactions are organized into a narrative structure of sequenceable stories rendered on axis-based graphical timelines, where artifacts, events, and collaborator states are indexed, linked, and tokenized. Behavioral signals extracted from the narrative context are used to (i) enrich prompt construction and retrieval-augmented generation, (ii) curate and contextualize training datasets, and (iii) propose context-aware AI agents and interventions. The storytelling interface aligns visual, temporal, and relational cues with machine-learning workflows to produce narratively grounded behavioral data for fine-tuning models and enabling context-sensitive information navigation.

sources.title: SYSTEM AND METHOD FOR ARTIFICIAL INTELLIGENCE BASED BEHAVIORAL FACIAL RECOGNITION [US20260351043A1]
sources.abstract: A system and method for integrating facial recognition with artificial intelligence (AI) behavioral analysis by analyzing facial images using micro-expressions, emotional markers and psychodynamic interpretations and generating an investigative dossier of behavioral facial recognition. Using a specially configured application-specific AI model and specific data architectures and data sets facial behavioral analysis is conducted that is capable of interpreting images (e.g., static images) of the human face and producing a detailed behavioral report by using micro-expressions, emotional markers and psychodynamic interpretations. Through the specially configured application-specific AI model a functional specialization process is deployed that combines supervised fine-tuning, instruction-based adaptation (i.e., instruction tuning) and integration of specialized domain knowledge wherein the AI model has a modular architecture comprised of multiple AI microservices that are specifically designed for the identification, classification and interpretation of behavioral facial traits.

sources.title: SYSTEMS AND METHODS FOR VISION-LANGUAGE MODELS OF AGENTIC OPERATIONS [US20260350361A1]
sources.abstract: Embodiments described herein provide a reinforcement learning (RL)-based framework to fine-tune VLMs for agent tasks such that the finetuned VLM may produce outputs that align with agent tasks (toward achieving success in the designated task) by optimizing the VLM's decision-making behavior within an environment. Specifically, the training framework may adopt offline RL techniques-filtered supervised fine-tuning (FSFT)—which selectively filters demonstration datasets using a learned value model. Unlike standard offline RL methods, the training framework uses FSFT to surpass its demonstrations while remaining identical to SFT when data quality is high. Additionally, FSFT enables seamless data collection for further improvement, making it a low-risk, high-reward alternative to SFT in VLM agent training

sources.title: DYNAMIC HYBRID MESH NETWORK UTILIZING DIGITAL ENHANCED CORDLESS TELECOMMUNICATIONS NEW RADIO+ (DECT NR+) AND LONG RANGE (LORA) NETWORKS [US20260353240A1]
sources.abstract: A method enabling dynamic data packet transfer in a mesh network of smart radio devices. A first smart radio device operating within a Digital Enhanced Cordless Telecommunications New Radio Plus (DECT NR+) network transmits a data packet to a wireless device using a first route, which includes multiple hops through several intermediate smart radio devices. Each device in the mesh network can dynamically switch between the DECT NR+ network and a Long Range (LoRa) network. While the data packet is being transmitted, signal strengths between the intermediate devices is continuously monitored. Responsive to a determination that a particular hop's signal strength falls below a predefined threshold, the method automatically switches the transmission for that hop from the DECT NR+ network to the LoRa network.

The method also includes identifying low-quality intervals in the input data having a quality that is below a quality threshold. Identifying the low-quality intervals includes determining a borehole rugosity based upon a first subset of the input data. The method also includes fine-tuning a pre-trained model based upon the low-quality intervals to produce a fine-tuned model.

The pretrained multimodal language model is fine-tuned to operate with the specific tools based on fine-tuning training data generated with a large language model separate from the pretrained multimodal language model. sources.title: QUANTUM-RESISTANT ATTESTED KEY AND MODEL LIFECYCLE MANAGEMENT SYSTEM [US20260352451A1]
sources.abstract: [0000]    A quantum-resistant system manages the key and model lifecycle of an artificial intelligence model within a trusted execution environment (TEE). A key management engine generates, seals, rotates, and revokes post-quantum keys bound to a hardware-rooted measurement. A secure model update module applies attested changes linking a prior state to a new state. A verifiable fine-tuning module binds, as a single signed unit, digests of training data, gradients, and resulting weights to the measurement. A tamper-evident provenance ledger records the operations and may anchor digests to a public blockchain. The system may mint a self-sovereign agent identity for consumption by a separate orchestration subsystem. Keys, updates, and evidence exist unencrypted only within the TEE and are tamper-evidently bound to the measurement, so an operator cannot alter or suppress them without invalidating the attestation.

sources.organization: SISVEL TECH S R L, UNIV DEGLI STUDI DI TORINO, INST MINES TELECOM
sources.abstract: A computer-implemented method for estimating the transferability of pruned neural network models for a downstream task, the method comprising: - receiving a plurality of pre-trained neural network models, each model having been pruned to reduce complexity; - for each pruned model, extracting feature representations from a dataset associated with the downstream task using the pruned model as an encoder; - applying a clustering algorithm to the extracted feature representations to form clusters corresponding to target classes, wherein the clustering algorithm operates without utilizing labels from the downstream task; - calculating a transferability score for each pruned model based on the alignment of the formed clusters with the known target classes, the transferability score being indicative of the model's suitability for the downstream task; - ranking the pruned models based on their respective transferability scores; selecting a pruned model from the ranked models as a candidate for deployment or further fine-tuning on the downstream task based on its transferability score.

sources.title: DYNAMIC CONTROL SYSTEM FOR COORDINATING PRODUCTION OF STREPTOMYCES SECONDARY METABOLITES AND USE THEREOF [WO2026228792A1]
authors: INST OF MICROBIOLOGY OF THE CHINESE ACADEMY OF SCIENCES
sources.organization: UNIV EAST CHINA SCIENCE & TECH, INST OF MICROBIOLOGY OF THE CHINESE ACADEMY OF SCIENCES
sources.abstract: The present invention provides a dynamic control system for coordinating the production of Streptomyces secondary metabolites and a use thereof. First, a universal artificial promoter PQS (trigger) responsive to multiple Streptomyces quorum-sensing systems is designed. A stabilizer is then constructed on the basis of a bistable gene circuit to convert transient signal output into stable signal output, thereby successfully eliminating dependence on inducers. Finally, an orthogonal amplifier is developed on the basis of a rare extracytoplasmic function σ factor of Streptomyces, and a library of different promoter elements responsive to the amplifier and spanning an approximately 535-fold strength range from weak to strong is constructed. The amplifier is combined with a CRISPRi system to construct an inverter, thereby achieving gene expression repression with a strength range of approximately 200-fold. The combination of the amplifier, the promoter library, and the inverter is referred to as an effector, providing abundant elements for fine-tuning target gene expression. The combination of the trigger, the stabilizer, and the effector is referred to as a Streptomyces multiplexed artificial control system (SMARTS), enriching control tools for Streptomyces.

sources.title: USING CONTEXT EXAMPLES DURING FINE-TUNING TO ADAPT GENERATIVE MODELS TO TASKS [US20260340414A1]
sources.abstract: Methods and systems are described for adapting a generative neural network to a downstream task by fine-tuning on augmented training data. A plurality of training examples is received, each including a training query and a target response. At each of a plurality of training steps, one or more current training examples are identified. For each of one or more training epochs at the training step, one or more context examples are selected for each current training example from a subset of the plurality of training examples that excludes the current training example. A modified training example is generated for each current training example, comprising the training query, a few-shot prompt that includes the selected context examples, and the target response. The generative neural network is then trained using the modified training examples.

sources.title: TRI-MATRIX LOW-RANK ADAPTATION OF ARTIFICIAL INTELLIGENCE OR MACHINE LEARNING MODELS [US20260340482A1]
sources.abstract: A system may utilize a fine-tuning operation to fine-tune a pre-trained artificial intelligence or machine learning (AI/ML) model. The system may generate a set of matrices that are indicative of a decomposition of a set of parameter weights associated with a task-specific parameters for the fine-tuning operation. The set of matrices may include one or more first matrices with one or more initialized values and a second matrix with one or more uninitialized values. The system may then train the second matrix to adjust the one or more uninitialized values. Moreover, the one or more initialized values of the second matrix may be associated with a subset of the task-specific parameters. Further, based on training the second matrix and a function, the system may obtain a fine-tuned model that includes a fine-tuned set of parameters associated with a fine-tuned set of parameter weights via the fine-tuning operation.

sources.title: Scientific Machine Learning Model Validation [US20260340411A1]
sources.abstract: Embodiments relate to validating machine learning models for scientific simulations. A system processes training data comprising geometric shapes to generate shape-based distance metrics. Input geometric data for a machine learning model is validated by comparing shape-based characteristics against the shape-based distance metrics to determine if the input falls within a predetermined distribution range of the training data. The system selectively processes the input geometric data using the machine learning model based on this determination. The validation may include converting geometric shapes into point cloud representations, performing nearest-neighbor mapping between points, and computing average distances between mapped points. For inputs outside the acceptable range, the system may route data to a simulation service that generates simulation results for fine-tuning the model.

sources.title: Low-Rank Adaptation for AI-Based Drug Discovery and Development [US20260340386A1]
sources.organization: ODAIBO STEPHEN GBEJULE, DEEP EIGENMATICS INC
sources.abstract: [0000]    Methods and systems are disclosed for fine-tuning a pre-trained neural network for an AI-based drug discovery and development task using low-rank adaptation. In one embodiment, a weight update matrix associated with a pre-trained weight matrix of the neural network is expressed as a summation of outer product matrices whose ranks form a composition of a selected low rank, the composition being uniform, non-uniform, or a single full-rank component. The outer product matrices are trained successively: an outer loop designates one outer product matrix at a time as a learnable parameter matrix while freezing the pre-trained weight matrix, and an inner loop iteratively updates the designated matrix until a stopping criterion is met, whereupon the trained matrix is added to the pre-trained weight matrix and a next outer product matrix is designated. The fine-tuned neural network generates candidate ligand representations, including peptides and small-molecule drugs for synthesis.

draft.summary: Research on supervised fine-tuning (SFT) has grown very quickly: OpenAlex works with the exact phrase rose from 615 in 2024 to 2,011 in 2025, and the year-to-date count is still rising (1,543 to 4,064). Filings show SFT sold as a product or service by Nvidia, Alibaba and small services firms, and patent publications mentioning fine-tuning are rising. The Science findings are mostly single-preprint, abstract-level claims that disagree on what makes SFT data effective (S1 vs S2). The Risk findings add that SFT degrades general ability through catastrophic forgetting, and that mitigations are unproven against each other. The patent counts are keyword-based and noisy (P6), and the exact-phrase paper counts are not normalised for overall publishing growth. The main uncertainty is whether SFT stays a core method as reinforcement-style and hybrid approaches take over parts of post-training; the evidence on this is thin and partial.
draft.plain_summary: Supervised fine-tuning is a way of teaching an existing AI model new skills by showing it many worked examples. Research and company activity around it are growing fast, and several large firms sell tools for it. The main thing that could hold it back is that the tuning can make models forget things they knew before, and newer training methods may take over some of its role.
